clinicalPearls: These disorders arise from defects in solute-carrier (SLC) family transporters; tissue distribution of the affected transporter and presence or absence of redundant transporters determine which organs (notably brain and sensory organs) are involved.

Cystinuria is an autosomal recessive defect of apical brush-border transport in the proximal renal tubule and small intestine, impairing reabsorption of the dibasic amino acids cystine, lysine, arginine, and ornithine; only poorly soluble cystine causes clinical disease through stone formation.

Cystine stones account for roughly 1-2% of all urinary calculi and about 4-5% of stones in children; suspect cystinuria when typical hexagonal crystals appear in acidified, concentrated, chilled urine or with a positive nitroprusside test.

Two cystinuria variants exist: type A (SLC3A1, a membrane glycoprotein) and type B (SLC7A9, the b0,+ transporter); the SLC3A1 glycoprotein aids correct processing of the b0,+ transporter, explaining why two different genes cause similar disease.

Lysinuric protein intolerance is a basolateral (not luminal) transport defect (SLC7A7, y+LAT transporter) affecting lysine, arginine, and ornithine but sparing cystine, with secondary impairment of the urea cycle and characteristic episodic hyperammonemia after protein loads or infection.

Citrullinemia type 2 (citrin deficiency, SLC25A13) reduces cytoplasmic aspartate available for the urea cycle and impairs the malate-aspartate NADH shuttle; affected individuals often spontaneously prefer protein/fat-rich foods and avoid carbohydrates, since carbohydrate-driven cytoplasmic NADH worsens the defect.

Hartnup disease is an autosomal recessive defect of the neutral/aromatic amino acid transporter B0AT1 (SLC6A19), which requires collectrin in kidney and ACE2 in intestine for surface expression; symptoms reflect tryptophan and consequent niacin deficiency.
In Hartnup disease only a minority of carriers of the transport defect become symptomatic, indicating that clinical expression depends on additional environmental and nutritional factors.

Cystinosis (CTNS gene; lysosomal cystine/proton transporter cystinosin) causes intralysosomal cystine accumulation and crystal formation; cystine crystals in the cornea on slit-lamp examination are an important diagnostic clue.

Cystinosis has three forms graded by residual transporter function: classic nephropathic (renal Fanconi syndrome with rickets in infancy, progressing to renal failure), juvenile nephropathic (proteinuria leading slowly to kidney failure), and ocular nonnephropathic (photophobia from corneal crystals as the only manifestation).

Citrin deficiency can present in infancy as neonatal intrahepatic cholestasis with failure to thrive and dyslipidemia, or in adulthood (typically ages 20-50) with recurrent hyperammonemic neuropsychiatric episodes resembling hepatic encephalopathy.

Most inherited amino acid transport defects are autosomal recessive; exceptions include certain neuronal/synaptic-vesicle glutamate transporter disorders (e.g., SLC1A2, SLC1A3, SLC17A8) that are autosomal dominant.
harrison.pathophysiology: Membrane transporters of the solute-carrier (SLC) superfamily move amino acids, peptides, sugars, ions, vitamins, water, and other molecules across plasma membranes and organelle membranes. Inherited loss of a transporter produces disease whose organ pattern depends on the transporter's tissue distribution and whether redundant transporters exist. In cystinuria, defective apical proximal-tubule and intestinal transport of dibasic amino acids leads to massive cystine excretion; because cystine is poorly soluble, it precipitates and forms stones. In lysinuric protein intolerance, a basolateral transport defect traps arginine inside cells and secondarily impairs the urea cycle, with proposed nitric-oxide-mediated immune dysfunction. In citrin deficiency, the mitochondrial aspartate-glutamate carrier defect limits cytoplasmic aspartate for argininosuccinate synthesis and impairs the malate-aspartate NADH shuttle, so a cytoplasmic NADH excess (worsened by carbohydrate) drives metabolic decompensation and hyperammonemia. In Hartnup disease, loss of the neutral amino acid transporter B0AT1 causes renal and intestinal malabsorption of tryptophan, producing functional niacin deficiency and pellagra-like features. In cystinosis, a defective lysosomal cystine/proton transporter causes intralysosomal cystine accumulation and crystal deposition throughout tissues, with the kidney (Fanconi syndrome, progressive renal failure) and cornea most prominently affected.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of urolithiasis (calcium, uric acid, struvite stones) versus cystine stones
Classic urea cycle defects versus the hyperammonemia of lysinuric protein intolerance and citrin deficiency
Dietary niacin deficiency versus Hartnup disease as a cause of pellagra
Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis versus the fatty liver seen in citrullinemia type 2
Other inherited causes of renal Fanconi syndrome versus nephropathic cystinosis
nonInfectiousMimics: Dietary niacin deficiency producing pellagra (mimics Hartnup disease but lacks neutral aminoaciduria)
Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis on liver histology (mimics citrin deficiency)
additionalInvestigations: Quantitative urinary amino acid analysis (selective overexcretion of cystine, lysine, arginine, ornithine in cystinuria; distinguishes heterozygotes from homozygotes)
Urinary nitroprusside test and microscopy for hexagonal cystine crystals in acidified, concentrated, chilled urine
Plasma and urine amino acids (low plasma lysine/arginine/ornithine with increased urinary excretion and orotic acid in lysinuric protein intolerance)

Genetic sequencing: SLC3A1/SLC7A9 (cystinuria), SLC7A7 (lysinuric protein intolerance), SLC25A13 (citrin deficiency, on hyperammonemia panels), SLC6A19 or CTLRN/collectrin (Hartnup disease), CTNS including deletion analysis (cystinosis)
During acute citrin deficiency attacks: ammonia, citrulline, arginine, glutamine, and red-cell galactose-1-phosphate
Slit-lamp corneal examination and white-blood-cell cystine content for cystinosis
redFlags: Episodic hyperammonemia with altered mental status, seizures, or coma in lysinuric protein intolerance or citrin deficiency (risk of cerebral edema and death)
Recurrent urolithiasis progressing to obstructive uropathy and renal insufficiency in cystinuria
Infantile renal Fanconi syndrome with rickets in nephropathic cystinosis (progression to renal failure by about age 10 without treatment)
Pellagra-like rash with neurologic relapse in Hartnup disease provoked by fever, sunlight, stress, or sulfonamides
Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, severe osteoporosis, or pancreatitis as adult presentations of lysinuric protein intolerance
harrison.prognosis: Prognosis is disorder-specific. Cystinuria can cause recurrent stones and occasional progression to renal failure requiring transplantation. Citrin deficiency, untreated, leads to death from cerebral edema within a few years in most symptomatic patients, but liver transplantation halts progression and normalizes biochemistry. In nephropathic cystinosis, life span was under 10 years before cystine-depleting therapy and transplantation; with current management affected individuals can survive into their late forties with satisfactory quality of life, though many still progress to end-stage renal disease and develop late multisystem complications.
pitfalls: Attributing pellagra solely to dietary niacin deficiency and missing Hartnup disease; neutral aminoaciduria distinguishes the two and does not occur in dietary deficiency.
Expecting elevated glutamine as in classic urea cycle defects in citrin deficiency, where glutamine is often low or normal during attacks.
Failing to recognize that cystinuria heterozygotes (especially type B) can have increased cystine excretion and may form stones, so quantitative measurement is needed.
Overlooking that only a minority of individuals with the Hartnup transport defect become symptomatic, so genotype does not equal disease.
Missing the carbohydrate-driven decompensation in citrin deficiency, where high sugar intake (and triggers such as acetaminophen, surgery, or alcohol) precipitates attacks.
harrison.severityClassification: Cystinosis is graded by residual transporter function into classic nephropathic (most severe, infantile Fanconi syndrome and early renal failure), juvenile nephropathic (proteinuria with slower decline to renal failure), and ocular nonnephropathic (photophobia from corneal crystals only). Cystinuria homozygotes excrete 2400-7200 micromol (600-1800 mg) cystine daily versus the maximum urinary solubility of roughly 1200 micromol/L (300 mg/L) at physiologic pH 4.5-7.0.
management: In cystinuria, reduce stone formation with high fluid intake, urinary alkalinisation using potassium citrate, and dietary sodium and animal-protein restriction
Add thiol-binding agents (tiopronin or penicillamine) for cystine stones refractory to conservative measures, and remove stones endoscopically or surgically as needed
In lysinuric protein intolerance, restrict dietary protein, supplement citrulline and use nitrogen-scavenging agents to prevent hyperammonaemic crises
In citrin deficiency, favour a protein- and fat-rich, carbohydrate-restricted diet with medium-chain triglyceride supplementation, and consider liver transplantation for progressive disease
In cystinosis, use the cystine-depleting agent cysteamine and provide renal replacement therapy or transplantation for established renal failure
Treat acute hyperammonaemic crises urgently with protein withdrawal, intravenous glucose and nitrogen-scavenging therapy, escalating to haemodialysis if severe
Offer genetic counselling and family screening for these autosomal recessive disorders, with multidisciplinary metabolic and nephrology follow-up
